## What Is a Recruiter?


A recruiter is the person responsible for finding, attracting, and hiring talent on behalf of a company or a candidate, sitting between organizations that need people and professionals looking for their next opportunity.


Recruiting involves more than posting a job and waiting. Recruiters source candidates actively, screen resumes, conduct initial interviews, coordinate the hiring process, and often negotiate offers. Some work inside companies directly; others operate through agencies or independently. The job requires equal parts people skills and process discipline.


> “Recruiting is sales, research, and project management rolled into one job title.”


Whether filling one role or scaling an entire team, a good recruiter shapes who gets hired and that shapes everything else.


## Types of Recruiters: Corporate, Agency, and Fractional Models


Not all recruiters work the same way. The model matters as much as the person, especially if you’re trying to figure out which type of recruiting support actually fits your situation.


### Corporate (In-House) Recruiters


These recruiters work directly for one company, usually full-time, embedded in the HR or people team. They know the culture deeply but only hire for that single organization.


### Agency Recruiters


Agency recruiters work for a staffing or search firm and serve multiple clients at once. They typically earn a commission tied to successful placements, which creates speed but can misalign incentives.


### Fractional Recruiters


Fractional recruiters operate on an hourly or part-time basis, functioning as an extension of a company’s team without the overhead of a full-time hire. Startups and growing companies often turn to this model when hiring volume isn’t consistent enough to support a full-time headcount but the need is too real to ignore.


Fractional recruiters work best when there is a shared ATS giving both the recruiter and the internal hiring team real-time visibility into candidate flow and sourcing activity. Without that shared infrastructure layer, coordination overhead multiplies and sourcing work can overlap. When the ATS and the recruiter operate in the same system, pipeline health stays visible and the recruiter can focus on finding and closing candidates instead of chasing status updates.

## What Does a Recruiter Do on a Daily Basis?


Most recruiting days follow a similar pattern: review applications, source passive candidates, run phone screens, coordinate interviews, and keep candidates moving through the pipeline. Other recurring tasks include reference checks, offer drafting, and tracking metrics like time-to-fill and offer acceptance rate. See the full breakdown of[core recruiting responsibilities](https://www.indeed.com/career-advice/career-development/recruiter-roles) for more detail.


The model shapes the priorities: agency recruiters spread their attention across multiple clients, corporate recruiters go deeper on fewer roles, and fractional recruiters focus on sourcing and closing since their time is billed by the hour. Across all three, response speed, clear communication, and respectful rejections shape how the employer is perceived in the talent market.


## Recruiter vs. Hiring Manager: Who Does What?


The two roles get conflated because both show up in the hiring process, but their responsibilities, accountability structures, and relationships with candidates are meaningfully different.


Dimension Recruiter Hiring Manager


Primary focus Sourcing, screening, and process management Assessing technical fit and making the final hire decision


Who they report to HR or Talent Acquisition leadership Business unit or department head


Candidate relationship Main point of contact throughout the process Engaged primarily during interviews and debrief


Compensation tied to Placements or salary (agency commission or base) Team performance and business outcomes


Role in offer Drafts and negotiates offer letter Approves headcount and compensation band


Both roles need to agree on role criteria before sourcing begins, or the process slows and candidate quality suffers. When recruiters and hiring managers run separate feedback loops, the process slows and candidate quality suffers.


## Recruiter Salary: What Do Recruiters Make in 2026?


Recruiter pay varies depending on where you sit in the profession. The average base salary in 2026 falls in the low-to-mid $60,000 range, with entry-level roles starting closer to $49,000 to $52,000 for those with under a year of experience. Recruiters in higher-cost markets like New York City or California often earn 20 to 30 percent above national averages, while those in lower cost-of-living markets may land below them. Agency recruiters frequently earn a lower base but stack commission on top, so total compensation can swing well above or below their in-house counterparts depending on the market.


Contract and fractional recruiters typically bill between $75 and $125 per hour. For a full-time recruiter on staff, loaded costs including salary, benefits, and overhead often run $85,000 to $170,000 annually.


## How to Become a Recruiter (With or Without a Degree)


Recruiting has no single required credential. Most job postings ask for a bachelor’s degree, but the field is full of people who came from sales, customer service, teaching, and other people-facing careers who found their footing without a traditional HR background.


What matters more than your degree is whether you can build rapport quickly, stay organized under pressure, and communicate clearly. Those skills transfer from almost anywhere.


To break in without experience, focus on a few concrete steps:


-


Get familiar with an ATS and common sourcing tools like[LinkedIn Recruiter](https://www.linkedin.com/products/linkedin-recruiter/) to show you understand the basic workflow of finding and tracking candidates.


-


Take a free or low-cost HR certification ([SHRM](https://www.shrm.org/credentials/certification/) , AIHR, or similar) to signal seriousness to hiring managers who might otherwise overlook your application.


-


Apply for coordinator or sourcing roles before jumping to full-cycle recruiter positions, since those entry points build credibility fast.


-


Offer to help a small business or startup with hiring, even informally, to build a track record you can reference in interviews.


Military experience is another legitimate path. The Army, Navy, and Air Force all have dedicated recruiter roles that provide structured training and real-world talent acquisition experience, often with a two to three year service commitment attached.


For most career changers, agency recruiting offers the fastest entry point, since many firms will hire people with strong communication skills and train them on the job.


## Specialized Recruiter Roles: Tech, Startup, and Industry-Specific Recruiting


Each recruiting niche demands a different skill set. Startup recruiters need to speak to equity and runway; tech recruiters need enough fluency to screen engineers credibly without being an engineer yourself. Other common specializations include executive search, healthcare and clinical staffing, legal and compliance, sales and go-to-market hiring, and diversity-focused recruiting. The narrower the niche, the higher the earning potential and the smaller the candidate pool you’re working with.


## Fractional Recruiters vs. Traditional Agencies: Cost and Model Comparison


Traditional agencies charge 15 to 25% of a candidate’s first-year salary. On a $120,000 hire, that’s $18,000 to $30,000 per placement. Fractional recruiters set their own hourly rates, which have typically fallen between $75 and $125 per hour, with most hires coming in between $2,000 and $7,000 in total.


The incentive structures differ too.[Agency recruiters get paid per placement](https://www.dover.com/blog/contingency-vs-hourly-recruiting-costs) , which can push toward speed over fit. Fractional recruiters working on top of shared ATS infrastructure keep all sourcing activity and pipeline data in the client’s system, removing the black-box dynamic common with traditional agencies. For companies making fewer than 15 to 20 hires per year,[fractional support often makes more sense](https://www.dover.com/blog/cost-of-hiring-agency-vs-in-house-vs-embedded-recruiting) than a full-time recruiter’s $85,000 to $170,000 loaded cost.


## Career Path and Job Outlook for Recruiters


Recruiting careers follow a recognizable ladder: most people start in coordinator or sourcing roles, move into full-cycle recruiting, and progress toward senior recruiter, talent acquisition manager, or VP-level leadership over time.


Job growth in the field is steady. The BLS projects HR specialist roles to grow roughly[8% through 2033](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/business-and-financial/human-resources-specialists.htm) , faster than average across occupations. Demand for technical and executive recruiters in particular remains strong as competition for specialized talent stays high.


AI tools (automated screening, chatbot-driven candidate outreach, and resume parsing) are moving recruiter time away from administrative tasks and toward higher-judgment work like assessment and closing. Recruiters who can prompt, configure, and quality-check those AI outputs are becoming more valuable than those who cannot. Relationship-building and candidate experience remain irreplaceable differentiators no matter how capable the tooling gets.

## FAQs


### What hiring tools do most YC startups actually use?


Seed-stage founders usually start with a lightweight ATS (Dover, Ashby’s free tier, or a shared spreadsheet) and LinkedIn Recruiter for sourcing. As teams grow past fifteen or twenty people, Ashby and Greenhouse become more common for their structured interview kits, while Lever suits growth-stage teams wanting a CRM-style workflow. Across YC alumni, the consistent pattern is that the ATS choice matters less than having someone accountable for running the process. Switching tools mid-hiring-push creates more disruption than most teams expect.


### How much does it cost to hire through a traditional agency vs. fractional recruiting?


Traditional agencies charge 15 to 25% of a candidate’s first-year salary, $18,000 to $30,000 for a $120,000 hire, paid regardless of how long the search took. Fractional recruiters set their own rates and bill hourly, typically $75 to $125 per hour, with most hires landing between $2,000 and $7,000 in total. Those are observed ranges rather than fixed prices, and they tend to make fractional support more cost-effective for companies making fewer than 15 to 20 hires per year.


### Do I need an ATS before bringing in a fractional recruiter?


Not strictly, but having one in place before a fractional recruiter starts makes the engagement considerably more productive. Without a shared ATS, the recruiter and internal team work from separate systems, which creates duplicate outreach, lost context, and no reliable view of pipeline health. With a shared ATS, the recruiter can source and move candidates while the internal team reviews in real time, with no coordination lag. Some tools pair a free ATS with fractional recruiter access in one system, which removes the setup friction of stitching together separate products.


## Final Thoughts on Understanding Recruiters


Asking “[what is a recruiter](https://www.dover.com/) ” matters when you’re hiring one or considering the profession yourself. The daily work looks similar across agency, corporate, and fractional models, but the incentives and cost structures create very different experiences for everyone involved. For teams that need real recruiting help without a full-time hire or agency fees, Dover offers fractional recruiters and a free ATS as a practical middle ground. The profession keeps growing because hiring the right people still shapes everything else.
